eligibility.evidence: Sec. 2.1 (p.3-4) and Sec. 4.2 (p.8-11): nine LLMs rate article credibility under a decoy manipulation that replicates a human crowdsourcing experiment; the decoy effect is a named classic paradigm and a human sample is run in the same paper.

A.title: The Decoy Dilemma in Online Medical Information Evaluation: A Comparative Study of Credibility Assessments by LLM and Human Judges
A.venue: arXiv preprint in ACM template (conference placeholder); record lists ACM TiiS

paradigms.name: Decoy effect on credibility ratings of COVID-19 treatment web pages (3 topics, SERP sessions)
paradigms.source_paper: decoy / asymmetric dominance effect; paper cites [66] Tversky & Kahneman 1985 in Sec. 2.1
paradigms.location: Sec. 4.1.2-4.1.3 (p.7-8): 40 TREC Health Misinformation pages per topic, decoy snippets written by the authors

D.population: Prolific participants: native English speakers, no medical training (UK 60.6%, US 25.3%); 617 completers reported in Sec. 4.1.1 versus 540 analysed in Sec. 4.1.4
D.metric: mean 5-point credibility rating of the target article, treatment versus control, independent t-test

E.headline: Decoy effects occur in both LLM and human credibility ratings but are more widespread in LLMs, especially GPT-4o and Claude-3-Sonnet with session-wide context.

G.notes: Human effect holds only in click and prior-knowledge subsets; the all-sessions t-tests are not significant. Temperature, query dates and the decoy snippets are not reported; no code link. Participant counts differ (617 versus 540). Decoy is an obviously false item, not asymmetric dominance. Single- versus multi-query context is the only variant.
